thermal.air-filter-location: three filters (left, center, right) on the front of the middle card cage

gaps.note: THESE BAY DIMENSIONS WERE GROWN TO MEET A COMPONENT AND ARE NOT MEASUREMENTS. Each was set by taking the size of a card the bay accepts, because a fit check reported the bay as too small. On this chassis: 42.67 on 20 bays - a9k-4hg-flex, 42.67 thick 403.10 on 20 bays - the 5th-generation envelope, 403.10 long The danger is specific and it is why they are listed rather than left to look like geometry. A fit check compares a bay to a component and NEITHER of them to the world, so it is satisfied by both being wrong together exactly as easily as by both being right. Every mismatch resolved by moving one side removes the signal without adding any truth, and once resolved nothing will flag it again. These are the entries where that happened, so the record survives the check going quiet. What IS independently grounded and is not in this list: the cage extents, measured off the stencil and confirmed on several chassis by printed slot labels or a card guide rail; the slot pitch; the 395.70 fourth-generation envelope, which is Cisco's own "includes ejector bracket/lever" figure; and the shapesheet sizes for the power modules and fan trays. The ejector arithmetic that explains why a bay legitimately exceeds its cage opening - 355.60 against 395.70, 40.10 mm - is also sourced, and it justifies the SHAPE of these numbers without justifying any particular one of them.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned figure giving the clear opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would replace every reconciled figure above with a measured one

gaps.note: A THIRD LINE OF EVIDENCE ON THE ~428 mm CONTROL CARDS, derived rather than asserted, and it comes from parts that have nothing to do with the question. The vertical space available to a card is bounded by whatever structure sits above and below its cage, and on this chassis that space measures the figure recorded in card-envelope-headroom below. A card envelope larger than that cannot be installed whatever any data sheet says, because something else is already there. Applied across the family: ASR 9010 399.96 mm between the cable management tray and the card guide bar ASR 9910 421.79 mm between the tray band and the front air intake ASR 9922 420.30 mm between the tray band and the fan band ASR 9912 439.21 mm - does NOT exclude 428.5, so this chassis is silent on the question ASR 9906 unbounded above in the model, so no constraint is derivable Three of the five independently exclude a 428.2-428.5 card. That is a separate argument from the slot pitch and from the ejector arithmetic, and it agrees with both. THE 9912 DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT and is recorded as silent rather than as agreement - a constraint that fails to bite is not evidence either way, and reporting it as if it were would manufacture support. The 9010's 399.96 also sits 3.14 mm under the 403.10 fifth-generation envelope its bays now carry, which is a smaller open question of the same kind.
gaps.wanted: a figure dimensioning the clear vertical opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would turn all of this from derived to measured

gaps.note: THE SECOND AXIS OF THE SAME CONFLICT, and it makes the first one much harder to explain away. The RSP-880 family is published at 428.5 mm on its long axis. Two Cisco statements fix what a line card measures on that axis in this family: Table A-10 of OL-17500-09 gives the original-generation card 14 in (355.60 mm) with NO qualifier, and the 4th-generation data sheets give 15.58 in (395.70) explicitly "including ejector bracket/lever". The 40.10 mm between them is the ejectors, about 20 mm each end - which is also why a bay declared at the 395.70 envelope is legitimately longer than the cage opening it sits in. Against that, 428.50 does not reconcile. Subtract the same 40.10 of ejector and the plate would still be 33.45 mm longer than this chassis's measured cage - a cage independently confirmed to 0.65 mm by Table A-10's own 355.60. So BOTH published RSP-880 dimensions, 46.0 thick and 428.5 long, are irreconcilable with a cage that two unrelated sources agree on. That is why the bays were NOT inflated to hold it. Building five chassis around a pair of numbers that contradict the only independently confirmed dimension in the family would put the error into the geometry instead of into the record. The accepts keep the RSP-880 where Cisco names it; the bays stay at what the cage and the reconcilable envelopes allow.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's plate dimensions as distinct from whatever 46.0 x 428.5 measures, or a photograph of an RSP-880 beside a line card

gaps.note: Cisco's RSP-880 and RSP880-LT data sheet gives "Height: 1.81 in. (4.60 cm)", i.e. 46.0 mm, and names the ASR 9006, 9010, 9904, 9906 and 9910 as the chassis they are the system processor for. THAT WIDTH EXCEEDS THE MEASURED SLOT PITCH ON EVERY CHASSIS IN THE FAMILY: 9010 44.33 9906 43.42 9910 43.78 9912 44.06 9922 44.06 and three of those pitches are measured from PRINTED SLOT LABELS or a card guide rail with a spread of 0.11 to 0.20 mm - among the best-supported numbers in this library. A card cannot be thicker than its slot, so 1.81 in is not the seating width; it is most likely taken over the ejector levers, the same way Cisco's line card "Width" is stated as "includes ejector bracket/lever" elsewhere. The accepts lists keep the RSP-880 family where Cisco names it, because a compatibility claim is Cisco's to make. The bays are sized to what the measured opening can hold. So a reader will find a bay narrower than a component it accepts, and that is a RECORDED CONFLICT between two sources rather than an oversight - the alternative was to inflate five chassis' geometry to fit one published number that three independent pitch measurements contradict.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's seating width as distinct from its over-ejector width, or any Cisco statement of an ASR 9000 slot pitch

gaps.note: The guide states that "line cards must be installed upside down in slots 10 through 19 of the bottom card cage, whereas in slots 0 though 9 of the top card cage, the line cards are installed right side up". This is a real property of the chassis and the model cannot currently express it. The bays for 10 to 19 are geometrically identical to 0 to 9 and carry no rotation, because the card is inverted about its own long axis rather than rotated in the plane of the panel - a `rotate: 180` would spin the faceplate end for end, which is a different thing and would put the ejectors at the wrong ends. So a card rendered in slot 15 will show its ports and its part number the same way up as one in slot 5, and on real hardware it would not. Anyone reading port positions off the lower cage should know that.
gaps.wanted: a mirror or flip transform on a bay, distinct from rotation, or a photograph settling exactly which way an inverted card reads

gaps.note: RP0 and RP1 are CUTOUTS rather than bays. The candidate component is cisco/asr-9922-rp-se/-tr, named for this chassis and carrying Table 23's "RP Card" figure of 259 W, but it declares a slot envelope of 46.0 mm and this cage's nine positions divide its measured 429.04 mm span into 47.67 mm each - which the RP would fit - while the LINE CARD cages divide into 43.388 and the rail pitch is 44.06. A 46.0 mm supervisor does not fit a 44 mm slot, and the same 46.0 x 428.5 x 628.9 appears on a9k-rsp880-se/-tr, byte for byte, which suggests one derivation reused rather than two measurements. Until that width is re-derived from the shapesheet these two positions stay openings. The seven fabric positions beside them ARE bays, because a99-sfc3's 41.4 fits comfortably.
gaps.wanted: a re-derivation of asr-9922-rp's width from the stencil shapesheet, both axes from one source

gaps.note: The four fan trays are cutouts. cisco/asr-9922-fan-v3 declares 475.96 mm wide and this chassis's BODY is 447.0, so the component is 29 mm wider than the box it goes in. Compare cisco/asr-9910-fan at 445.2, which sits inside its own 447 mm body correctly. Both are class cooling and one of them is measured against the rack face rather than the body - the stencil records rack-face widths for trays and covers, and 475.96 is within a few millimetres of the 482.6 mm rack face. The openings here are the measured bands and the component is not placed.
gaps.wanted: asr-9922-fan-v3's width re-derived against the body, or confirmation that the fan tray really does span the rack face and needs a negative offset like a mounting ear

gaps.note: THE BOTTOM IS THE ONLY FACE OF THIS CHASSIS WITH NO SOURCE, and it is not a gap in this file's research. There is no bottom view of ANY ASR 9000 chassis anywhere in the 78-document intake: every figure caption in all 65 PDFs was searched for "Bottom View", "underside" and "bottom of the chassis", and the result is zero hits. That is a fact about how Cisco documents a rack chassis rather than about this model - a face that sits on rack rails and is never serviced gets no figure. The face is SIZED correctly from Table 13, so a rack elevation and the 3D box are the right shape; what it lacks is any statement of what is on it. Nothing is invented to fill it, and no region is added naming the absence, because a check passed by annotating that you have nothing is worse than a check failed honestly. THIS HOLDS THE CHASSIS AT CAPABILITY 2. Front, rear, top, left and right all now carry sourced content; the bottom alone does not, and level 3's implementation requires content on all six. The written design asks only that six faces be "present, sized, and mutually consistent", which this file satisfies - the content requirement comes from `_has_content`, which was written for level 1. See working/notes/deliberately-empty-faces.md.
gaps.wanted: a bottom elevation, a photograph of the underside, or a way for a view to declare itself deliberately empty so that empty-by-verification counts where empty-by-omission does not

a `power-draw-max-w` on each module this chassis accepts, from the vendor's own per-card table - Cisco publishes one per ambient, most vendors publish none, and until they land a module total is a floor

a top-level `profile:` naming the device class, so that `specified` has something to judge the attrs against - see spec/schemas/profiles.yaml for the classes that exist, which unlocks `specified` and with it the About panel, and comparison against other devices
ports the Nautobot exporter recognises - each port placement needs `attrs.media` and `attrs.speed` in a combination it maps - unlocks NetBox / Nautobot device-type export

provenance.air-filter: datasheet - Table 17, b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf p228: "Three air filters located on the front of the middle card cage". The guide adds that on this chassis and the 9912 "the three air filters (left, center, and right) contain foam media" and can be removed individually. Not modelled - no figure dimensions them
provenance.airflow: datasheet - "Cisco ASR 9922 Router: Front-to-rear cooling path. The inlet is at the front of the middle cage, and the exhaust is at the upper and lower rear", b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf p3737. Unique in the family for exhausting at BOTH ends
provenance.bay-opening-is-the-hole-not-the-reserved: `size` on these bays is what the slot RESERVES - where a card is placed and what L33 and L34 check it against - and it is the card's own envelope, per the arbitration that a bay and its occupant carry the same size. The renderer also painted that rectangle dark, so the visible opening was drawn over sheet metal at each end of every slot. `opening` now carries the hole separately: 358.17 and 355.75 mm, THREE cages, and they are not the same height. The upper and lower line-card cages measure y 367.83 to 726.00 and 1422.99 to 1781.15; the RP and fabric cage between them is y 898.83 to 1254.58, very slightly shorter, which is why it carries its own figure rather than the line cards'. NOTHING ABOUT PLACEMENT OR CHECKING MOVES. Only what is painted dark changes, and the opening is centred on the bay because a hole and the space reserved around it share a centre. Where only one axis is measured the other keeps the bay's own figure rather than being inferred from the occupant, which is the mistake this field exists to undo.
provenance.bottom-face: datasheet - the bottom is NOT featureless after all, and the feature is the one thing every footprint figure dimensions. Figure 13 dimensions 22 in (55.88 cm) from the rear. The rack mounting flange is a vertical plate spanning the chassis height, so it intersects the BOTTOM plane as well as the top and appears on this face as a line across the width at that depth. That is a real dimensioned feature rather than an annotation of absence, which is the distinction that matters here - an earlier revision of this file said the bottom was unreachable without inventing something, and that was wrong. What remains true is that no BOTTOM VIEW of any ASR 9000 chassis exists in the 78-document intake; what this face carries is a feature dimensioned in a TOP-down figure whose geometry the bottom necessarily shares. Positions are given from the REAR, which is how the figures dimension them
provenance.cage-geometry: drawing - three cages measured off the front master. Upper line cards y 367.83 to 726.00, lower line cards y 1422.99 to 1781.15, both spanning x 6.36 to 440.24. The RP/FC cage sits between them at y 898.83 to 1254.58, spanning x 8.98 to 438.02 - very slightly narrower, which is why its nine positions are divided on their own span rather than on the line card cages'
provenance.calibration: measured - gate 1 passed. Calibrating x on 482.6 mm (the 19.0 in rack face) and y on Table 13's 1955.8 mm independently gives 0.20134 and 0.20144 mm/px, agreeing to 0.05 percent
provenance.card-compatibility: datasheet - c78-743580's "Chassis compatibility" row names this chassis: "Compatible with the Cisco ASR 9006, ASR 9010, ASR 9904, ASR 9906, ASR 9910, ASR 9912, and ASR 9922 chassis". Those four flex cards go in all twenty line card bays with the blank. The seven fabric bays take cisco/a99-sfc3@1, which Table 23 names as "A99-SFC3 Card (ASR 9922)" - this chassis by name, and the 340 W it carries is this chassis's figure rather than the 9912's lower one
provenance.card-envelope-headroom: derived - 420.30 mm of clear vertical space between the structure above this card cage and the structure below it, measured off this chassis's own committed geometry. Any card envelope larger than that cannot be installed regardless of what its data sheet states. Used as a check on the control-card lengths, not as a source for the bays
provenance.card-orientation: datasheet - "Cisco ASR 9922 Router: All RP, FCs, and LCs are front-facing and mounted vertically, with ejector levers and captive screws at the top and bottom of each card" (Chassis Slots, p17). So every bay places its component unrotated
provenance.cards-upside-down: datasheet - a real fact about this chassis that no drawing shows and nothing in the model can express yet. The guide states: "For the Cisco ASR 9922 Router, line cards must be installed upside down in slots 10 through 19 of the bottom card cage, whereas in slots 0 though 9 of the top card cage, the line cards are installed right side up" (p26). The bays for slots 10 to 19 are geometrically identical to 0 to 9 and carry no rotation, because the card is inverted in its own plane rather than rotated in the panel's - see gaps
provenance.chassis: datasheet - Table 13, b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf p130. ASR 9922: chassis height 77.00 inches (195.58 cm), chassis width 17.60 inches (44.70 cm) with "19.0 inches (48.3 cm) including chassis rack-mount flanges and front door width", chassis depth 26.3 inches (66.82 cm), "30.00 inches (76.20 cm) including the cable management system" and "30.62 inches (77.77 cm) with front doors". Modelled as the BODY, 447.0 x 1955.8 x 668.0 mm
provenance.compliance: datasheet - data_sheet_c78-501767.pdf series compliance list, transcribed as printed
provenance.electrical: datasheet - Table 15 (AC) and Table 16 (DC), pp132-135, ASR 9922 columns only
provenance.environmental: datasheet - Table 14, p131. The 9922 is in the narrower short-term group, 23 to 122 degF (-5 to 50 degC)
provenance.faces-verified-independently: THIS CHASSIS WAS HELD BACK UNTIL ITS FACES WERE SETTLED, because Cisco's ASR 9910 masters are named front and rear the wrong way round and an unverified face is not a face. Three independent checks now agree that asr-9922-front IS the front. FIRST, the guide states it: "Cisco ASR 9922 Router: All RP, FCs, and LCs are front-facing and mounted vertically, with ejector levers and captive screws at the top and bottom of each card" (Chassis Slots, p17). SECOND, this master carries the CABLE MANAGEMENT TRAY with its diagonal cable slots, which is front-face furniture on every chassis in this family. THIRD, its band order reproduces Figure 24 exactly - power shelves, line card cage, a fan pair, the RP/FC cage, a second fan pair, the lower line card cage. The concern that first held it back, that the master named `-rear` shows power modules where Figure 24 puts them on the front, is explained by the power system being at the TOP and reachable from both faces
provenance.fan-band-pitch: drawing - the upper pair FT0 and FT1 sit at 762.30 and 808.80 mm, a 46.5 mm pitch. The lower pair is placed on the same pitch from the measured start of its band, 1276.90 and 1323.40. An earlier revision put FT3 at 1317.40, taken from a rule in the band scan that turned out to be internal detail rather than the tray's top edge, and the two openings overlapped by a millimetre - they rendered as one solid bar. LINT DID NOT SEE IT because L13 compares BAYS and these are cutouts, so overlapping holes in the metal are not checked. Only the render showed it
provenance.first-generation-fabric-accepted: datasheet - the fabric bays gain this chassis's first-generation switch fabric card, placed on the component's own attrs.chassis, which names exactly one chassis. That single-chassis declaration is why it can be added without a compatibility row: the part says where it goes
provenance.four-hg-flex-accepted: datasheet - the A9K-4HG-FLEX and A99-4HG-FLEX pairs added to the line card slots, and each is placed on ITS OWN declared chassis list rather than on an inference from generation. The A9K pair's contract names all seven chassis; the A99 pair's names five - "ASR 9922, ASR 9912, ASR 9910, ASR 9906 and ASR 9904" - so the two are not interchangeable even though they share an envelope. A component that declares what it fits is a better source than a chassis deciding what it will take
provenance.four-port-100ge: datasheet - c78-740092's "Chassis compatibility" row: "Compatible with the Cisco ASR 9006, ASR 9010, ASR 9904, ASR 9906, ASR 9910, ASR 9912, and ASR 9922 chassis". All seven, stated outright, and the component's own attrs.chassis carries the same list. At 41.4 mm it fits every line card bay in the family. Added to the line card slots only - a compatibility row names a chassis, not a slot, and this chassis's RSP and RP positions take supervisors
provenance.grounding: datasheet - "Top rear right side of the chassis", b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf p125, illustrated by Figure 136. The same corner as the ASR 9006's, and unlike the 9010, 9910 and 9912 which put theirs at the bottom
provenance.lifecycle: datasheet - searched. No end-of-sale or end-of-life notice for this chassis was found
provenance.no-chassis-power-figure: NOTE, and NARROWED. The current Table 14 says only to use the Cisco Power Calculator, so there is no chassis-level figure for THIS chassis in any document held, and the module total here is a floor. That is narrower than what an earlier revision of this file claimed: it said Cisco publishes no chassis draw for ANY ASR 9000, and that is false. The older Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide (asr9kELCIGbk.pdf, OL-17500-09) states "Power Dissipation 7600 W maximum (Cisco ASR 9010 Router)" and 4556 W maximum for the ASR 9006 in its Table A-1 - a table the current revision deleted. Those two chassis predate this one and no equivalent figure for this model appears in either revision, so this is the vendor being silent about this chassis rather than about the family
provenance.power-module-columns: the four columns are placed on the cover's 105.05 mm column pitch, CENTRED in the body. That centring is an assumption: the cover is a rack-face part 475.12 mm wide and this chassis's body is 447.0, so its column origin cannot be read straight across. Four columns at 105.05 span 420.2, leaving 13.4 mm each side of a 447 body, which is a plausible margin but is arithmetic rather than measurement
provenance.power-module-width-corrected: datasheet - the sixteen module bays were 95.85 x 42.80 and are now 99.62 x 42.85, the shapesheet figure for BOTH axes. 95.85 was the same mixed-source error the ASR 9006 and 9010 power bays carried - a shapesheet height with an art-derived width - and asr9k-cards corrected the component after I found three of them would not fit a shelf that holds three. This chassis was missed when the others were swept, because its power bays are sixteen in a grid rather than three in a row and my sweep matched on the row form. Found by asr9k-cards' fit check, which compares every bay against every component it accepts; nothing in lint sees a bay narrower than its occupant
provenance.power-shelves: measured, and the component confirms it. The top band measures 0.20 to 193.40 mm - 193.2 mm for four shelves, so 48.3 mm each. cisco/a9k-power-shelf-cover, built independently from the stencil's own 'Power Shelf Cover' master, is 193.7 mm tall with SIXTEEN positions PM0 to PM15 on a 48.7 mm row pitch and a 105.05 mm column pitch. 193.2 against 193.7, and sixteen positions against this chassis's four shelves of four. That settles what had been an open question about which chassis that master belongs to: it is this one. Table 15 agrees on the count - "Version 2 power system: Up to sixteen AC power modules per system, four per tray"
provenance.ru: datasheet - 77.00 in / 1.75 = exactly 44.00 RU, and the stencil's height_in of 7.7006 agrees
provenance.side-and-top-faces: datasheet - NAMED but not dimensioned, and drawn as regions rather than decor for that reason. Figure 13 (the chassis footprint figure in b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf) shows the top plate outline and the rack mounting brackets, and Figure 76 (the chassis cooling path side view) shows the airflow through the side. Both name what is on those faces; NEITHER dimensions any feature on them, so nothing here carries coordinates. Contrast the ASR 9906, whose HIG Figure 17 gives explicit rail positions at 9.45 in and 5.00 in from the rear and where those rails ARE drawn. The distinction is deliberate: a region says "this is here" and decor says "this is here, at this size, in this place", and only the second needs a dimension behind it
provenance.side-face-labels-say-when-a-position-is-: every region on a side face now states either where the feature sits or that no figure dimensions it. That second half is the point. A region reading only "Vertical rack rail locations" is silent about position, and silence is indistinguishable from a position that was known and not written down - which is exactly how a feature ends up drawn at the wrong end with nothing to contradict it. casa-cards found seven such features across two chassis where the LABEL WAS RIGHT AND THE GEOMETRY WAS WRONG, and lint stayed green because no rule compares the two. Saying "present but not dimensioned" gives a reader the same thing a distance would: a claim to check the drawing against
provenance.slot-pitch: measured, and NOT taken from the card guide rail on this chassis even though the rail is there. Its ten rail bolts give a pitch of 44.06 with a spread of 0.11 mm, identical to the ASR 9912's and confirming the two are one mechanical build. But those bolts are NOT aligned to slot centres here: taking them as centres puts slot 0 thirteen millimetres inside the cage and slot 9 eighteen millimetres past its right edge, which is asymmetric in a way the 9912's are not. So the bays divide the MEASURED CAGE evenly - 433.88 over ten is 43.388 - and the rail is used only as corroboration that this generation's pitch is about 44. That asymmetry is what stopped this chassis being built on the rail, and it is the same check that caught the 9910's swapped faces and my own mislabelling of these bolts as printed slot IDs
provenance.slots: datasheet - Figure 24 "Cisco ASR 9922 Router Slot Numbering", p39 of b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf, read at 250 dpi. Top to bottom: power shelves PS0 to PS3 each M0 to M3; the upper line card cage, Slot 0 to Slot 9 carrying LC0 to LC9; fan trays FT0 and FT1; a cage of nine positions named RP0, FC0 to FC6, RP1; fan trays FT2 and FT3; and the lower line card cage, Slot 10 to Slot 19 carrying LC10 to LC19. As on the ASR 9912 the RP and FC positions are named by Cisco rather than numbered, so they are named here too
provenance.strip-is-centred-on-the-plane: the rack mounting strip is 3.9 mm thick and is placed so the DIMENSIONED PLANE PASSES THROUGH ITS MIDDLE, at y = plane - 1.95. Neither edge carries the number. An earlier revision put the plane on one edge, which meant the figure's dimension was 3.9 mm from where the drawing said it was, and which edge differed between chassis - casa-cards found the same inconsistency across the two it owns and centred them the same way
provenance.strip-label-carries-the-number: the region label states the figure's own dimension AND its conversion to a distance from the front. That is not decoration: it is the only number in the file a reader can check the geometry against, and its absence is why the ASR 9906's strips sat in the wrong half of the box through two reviews before a human noticed. Where the label carried a distance - on the ASR 9006 and 9904 - the same error was caught in minutes
provenance.top-and-bottom-agree: the rack mounting flange is one vertical plate, so it intersects the top and bottom planes at the SAME depth and appears on both faces at the same y. An earlier revision drew it only on the bottom, which left the two faces of one chassis disagreeing about where the chassis bolts to the rack - the kind of internal inconsistency this work has spent the night finding in other people's artefacts. casa-cards' ASR 9006 and 9904 match across both faces and are the standard this follows
provenance.top-and-bottom-view-convention: ON THIS CHASSIS'S TOP AND BOTTOM VIEWS, y = 0 IS THE REAR AND y = depth IS THE FRONT. Verified on this chassis's own footprint figure rather than carried across from a sibling: the figure prints "Rear of chassis" above the drawing and "Front of chassis" below it, read by eye because that text is vector art and does not extract. Stated here because it is not derivable from the file and because reading it the other way turns every depth-wise position into its complement - which is exactly the error that put this family's ASR 9906 strips in the wrong half of the box.
provenance.twelve-port-100ge: datasheet - c78-737623's "Chassis compatibility" row reads "Compatible with the Cisco ASR 9904, ASR 9910, ASR 9912, and ASR 9922 chassis". This chassis is named, so cisco/a99-12x100ge@1 joins the line card bays. NOTE WHICH CHASSIS IS ABSENT: the ASR 9906. That card goes in every other 9900-generation chassis and not in the 9906, which is the second time a Cisco compatibility row has singled that chassis out, and exactly why these lists are transcribed rather than inferred from generation
provenance.weight: datasheet - Table 13. "Chassis only - 300 pounds (136 kg)" and "Chassis: fully configured using all card slots and four power modules - 1038 pounds (470.28 kg)". Note "four power modules" against sixteen bays; Cisco's phrasing in this column is not consistent across the family
